coachMessages.text: Gray has one strong threat. Green blocks it. What did Gray accomplish?

slides.infoProse: One threat gives your opponent a simple task: block it. They use one move, your attack is over, and you have gained nothing. To guarantee a win, you need your opponent to face a problem they cannot fully solve in a single move.

coachMessages.text: One move, two threats. Gray must answer — but one reply can only cover one of them.

legendItems.label: Green's two threat cells (Gray can only block one)

slides.infoProse: A fork is a single move that creates two simultaneous threats. Your opponent has one turn to respond — they can block one threat, but the other remains. On your next move, you win. The key: both threat cells must be immediately reachable (at the top of their column's current stack).

coachMessages.text: Forks don't have to point left and right. Two threats can stack in the same column — and blocking the bottom one hands Green the top.

legendItems.label: Green's stacked threat cells (two pairs, one per side)

slides.infoProse:
Forks are not always spread across two different columns. When two threats complete in the same column on adjacent rows, blocking the lower one gives Green the upper one — the block itself becomes the setup. This board actually holds two such stacked pairs, one in the first column and one in the fifth: whoever finds either pair has found the same pattern.

One important caution: all four of these cells sit high above empty squares — none of them is playable yet, so this is NOT a fork Green can cash today. It is a trap that wins later, as the columns underneath fill up. The Z-Threats and Figure-7 lessons build on exactly this idea.

coachMessages.text: This looks like a fork — but are both threat cells actually reachable right now? Check the column heights before celebrating.

legendItems.label: Future threat (not reachable yet - not a fork)

slides.infoProse: A fork only works when both threats are immediately reachable — at the top of their column's current stack. A position with one real threat and one future threat is not a fork: your opponent blocks the immediate threat and has plenty of time to deal with the buried one later. Always verify that both threat cells are playable on the very next move.

socratic.goalPrompt: Green to move. Playing the fifth column makes three green discs in a row on the bottom row with open squares at both ends (second and sixth columns) — a fork Gray cannot fully block. Solver: the fork move is the unique best move (+16); every other column is strictly worse.
socratic._boardInstructions: Board from movestring 33333026 (solver-verified 2026-07-24). Green (to move) has bottom-row discs in columns 3 and 4 (1-based); column 4 also carries an alternating tower up to row 5. Gray has lone bottom-row discs in columns 1 and 7. Playing the fifth column lands Green on the bottom row, making three in a row across columns 3-5 with BOTH completing squares open and immediately playable: bottom of column 2 and bottom of column 6 (marked with 'claim' overlays — before the move they are only minor threats, so they are amber attention markers, not threat dots). Gray has no gravity-top threat anywhere. Solver scores pre-move: [-3,1,3,-3,16,3,-2] — column 5 (1-based) is the unique max and wins.
